peak_era: 12c–17c as volume king of Oriental spices
modern_status: still a large bulk spice but no longer a geopolitical prize
historical_role: Late-medieval Europe's main Oriental spice by volume and the cream of Italian long-distance trade. Venice re-exported thousands of tons annually; a pound cost more than two days' skilled wages in 15c England. Direct sea access to pepper (Calicut 1498) was a primary motive of the Portuguese Cape route.
notes: Flagship of Spices (value 18). Splitting gives a recognisable import on Europe maps. Keep demandCoverage thin if Spices remains.

historical_role: Dearer than black pepper in medieval Europe; later lost the market.
notes: Flavour only.

historical_role: Second-rank medieval spice after pepper/ginger. Ceylon cinnamon was a Portuguese then Dutch prize.
notes: Split if Ceylon-vs-China flavour is wanted; else keep under Spices.

historical_role: Grown only in the Moluccas until the French and British smuggled seedlings. VOC enforced monopoly by force and destroyed surplus trees. A pound cost nearly five days' skilled wages in 15c England.
notes: Best single good for a 'Spice Island monopoly' story.

historical_role: The narrowest luxury monopoly in the early-modern world. Bandanese society was destroyed to secure it. Mace is the aril of the same fruit.
notes: Pair with cloves. Mace can be a byproduct rather than its own Good.

historical_role: Same tree as nutmeg; sold separately at a premium.
notes: Byproduct of Nutmeg if nutmeg is split.

historical_role: Household accounts (e.g. Duke of Buckingham) used pepper and ginger daily. Less geographically locked than cloves/nutmeg.
Persistent but never the volume king.
Early Atlantic substitute while the Cape route was opening.
notes: Useful as a West African cargo flavour.

historical_role: Java pepper; medieval apothecary spice.

typical_origin: Mexico; later Réunion/Madagascar after hand pollination
historical_role: Mesoamerican orchid. Commercial production outside Mexico required hand pollination. Complements cacao.
notes: Or leave under Spices. Distinctive enough to stand alone.

historical_role: Transformed Old World cooking but is not a lasting long-haul import once naturalised.
notes: Do not register as an extra-European import.

typical_origin: Yemen (Mocha) then Java then Caribbean then Brazil
modern_status: one of the world's top tropical commodities
historical_role: Yemeni mocha reached Europe in the 17c; estate cultivation then moved to Java, Bourbon, and the Antilles. Coffee houses were information exchanges. Brazil later made it a bulk staple.
notes: 04 draft: value 10, highland biome 3/5/7. On Europe maps use chance 0 plus import stock.

historical_role: Core of the 18c China trade and the tea duties that helped spark the American Revolution. 19c plantations in Assam and Ceylon broke the China monopoly.
notes: Already value 10. Current distribution almost never fires on Europe maps.

historical_role: Drink of Mesoamerican elites; European chocolate houses in the 17c–18c. Modern supply shifted to West Africa.
notes: 04 draft: value 12, biome(7). chance 0 on Europe maps.

required_climate: warm temperate to tropical; grows in biome 6
historical_role: Virginia's cash crop and a triangular-trade return cargo. Not strictly climate-locked in Europe.
notes: Current distribution includes temperate deciduous forest.

typical_origin: Mediterranean fringe then Atlantic islands then Brazil/Caribbean
modern_status: bulk; beet sugar competes in Europe
historical_role: Heart of the Atlantic plantation economy and the triangular trade. Displaced honey as the European sweetener.
notes: Rum = Liquor recipe on Sugarcane. Beet sugar is the European substitute and should stay a separate local path if added.

required_climate: mulberry can grow in Mediterranean; current Good is biome(7)
historical_role: The classic compact Asian luxury. Mediterranean sericulture never fully replaced Chinese and later Japanese export silk.
notes: On Europe maps the biome(7) lock already makes it an import. Do not loosen distribution.

historical_role: Indian calico sparked a European consumer revolution and import bans. Raw cotton then fed the industrial revolution.
notes: Southern Europe may just qualify. Finished calico is Cloth with a Cotton recipe.

required_climate: Indian weaving skill more than climate
historical_role: Printed Indian cotton undercut European woollens and triggered protectionism.
notes: Do not add a separate Good; add { Cotton: 1 } to Cloth if missing.

historical_role: Cheap sacking for grain wool and cotton cargoes. A Dundee–Bengal industrial pair.
notes: Industrial-era gate. Low value high bulk.

typical_origin: India then Carolina then India again
historical_role: Replaced European woad as the standard blue. A plantation dye and a major EIC/Atlantic cargo.
notes: 04 draft value 9. Keep Dyes as local madder/woad. Optional Garments recipe variant.

peak_era: 16c–19c (second only to silver among some New Spain exports)
historical_role: Scarlet dye; the process was a guarded secret. Far higher value density than vegetable dyes.
notes: Register only if scarlet-vs-blue dye politics is wanted.

historical_role: Named Brazil. Early Portuguese Atlantic dye cargo before sugar took over.
Black/purple dye; Bay of Honduras logging camps were a geopolitical irritant.
Red lac dye and later a varnish/electrical insulator.
Church and apothecary demand. The incense road predates the spice boom.
notes: Already value 12. Distribution is desert/hot forest.

historical_role: Perfume wood and carving material. Timor sandalwood was an early European eastern cargo.
notes: Or keep under Incense.

historical_role: Rarer than frankincense; incense and medicine.
Medicine mothproofing and later celluloid. A distinctive East Asian cargo.
Animal perfume in the same luxury class as ambergris and civet.
notes: Perfume already exists as a finished Good.

historical_role: Burned against plague miasma; extreme perfume ingredient.
notes: Do not confuse with Amber (Baltic fossil resin — European).

historical_role: The only reliable malaria prophylactic of the empire age. Seed smuggling to Java created a Dutch plantation monopoly.
notes: Strategic medicinal. 17c+ gate.

required_climate: poppies grow in Europe; Bengal was the trade source
typical_origin: India (Bengal/Malwa) to China; also medicine in Europe
historical_role: Historically huge but not climate-locked for Europe. Europe was more a re-exporter and a medical consumer than a climate importer.
notes: Skip unless a China-trade scenario is modelled.

historical_role: Early New World wonder drug; quickly faded.
Vulcanisation made it an industrial necessity (tyres waterproofing insulation). Wickham's seeds shifted production to SE Asia.
notes: 04 draft value 8 biome(7). Disable on medieval maps. chance 0 on Europe maps.

required_climate: Palaquium trees of the Malay world
historical_role: The only practical deep-sea cable insulator of the 19c. Transatlantic and imperial cables depended on it. Harvesting felled wild trees.
notes: Do not fold into Rubber; the use-case and era are unique.

modern_status: one of the largest tropical commodities
historical_role: Replaced tallow in soap and lubricated early industry. 20c–21c food and oleochemical staple.
notes: Industrial and modern gates. High bulk low value.

historical_role: Dried coconut meat for oil and soap.
notes: Can sit under Palm oil if catalogue space is tight.

historical_role: Prestige cabinet wood. Already in GOODS_DATA.
notes: value 10. Almost never places on Europe maps.

historical_role: Deck and structural timber that resists rot better than European oak in the tropics.
notes: Or keep under Mahogany as tropical timber.

historical_role: Inlay and instrument wood. 04 already maps ebony onto Mahogany.

required_climate: kaolin plus high-fire kilns; knowledge lock
historical_role: Paid for with New World silver via Manila. Europe treated it as a precious good until it learned the recipe.
notes: 04 draft value 14. chance 0; not a biome good. Ceramics stays the common ware.

required_climate: tropical elephants (walrus is a northern substitute)
historical_role: Carving and luxury inlay. Current Good is an Elephant recipe so it will not appear without elephants.
notes: value 35. Do not add a wild scatter on Europe maps.

historical_role: Compact high-value cargo on the medieval Alexandria–Venice route.
notes: Needs coral/warm-shore habitats.

typical_origin: tropical/subtropical reefs; some Med. red coral
historical_role: Jewellery and reliquary material.
Combs inlays and luxury furniture veneer.
Military prestige animal. Already climate-locked to biomes 1/3/5/7.
Desert transport. Appears if the Europe map has desert.
notes: Not extra-European if Andalusia-like desert exists.

historical_role: Already treated as a Middle Eastern chest import in value notes.
Medieval Europe imported rice as a luxury. Wet-rice heartlands are extra-European.
notes: 04 draft exists. Not a hard lock on the far south.

typical_origin: Caribbean / Central America after 19c refrigerated shipping
historical_role: Became a mass European food only with steamships and refrigeration.
notes: Modern gate. Poor medieval cargo (spoilage).

typical_origin: Chincha Islands (Peru) and other Pacific islands
historical_role: Best natural nitrogen fertiliser of the mid-19c. Peruvian state monopoly; Chincha War and later Pacific War. Suggested as a blight vector to Ireland.
notes: 19c-only. High bulk. Strategic for ag-tech once that system exists.

historical_role: Currency good more than a European consumer import.
notes: Useful only if African trade is modelled.

historical_role: First global currency metal. Manila galleons paid for silk and porcelain.
notes: Do not add a new Good; seed extra-European silver into port markets.

historical_role: Trans-Saharan gold paid for salt and manufactures before the Atlantic reroute.
India supplied Europe until Brazilian then South African rushes.
Successor to guano. Pacific War prize. Feeds Saltpeter/Gunpowder.
Current Oil Good is mostly olive/whale. Extra-European crude needs a separate source or a retagged mineral Oil.
notes: Modern. Do not grow biome Oil on Europe farmland.

historical_role: Industrial tinplate and canning.
Columbian crop that naturalised and changed European demography. Not an import good after introduction.
notes: Already local food. postMedieval tag is the right handle.

required_climate: warm temperate — grows in southern Europe
historical_role: High-yield naturalised grain. Not a long-haul luxury.
notes: 04 draft is for local biome output not import.

historical_role: A month's skilled wages per pound in 15c England — but it is a European crop.
notes: Do not treat as extra-European.

historical_role: Temperate extra-European; Europe can grow wool.
Latitude-compatible with Europe. Siberian/Canadian furs are geographic not climatic outsiders.
notes: Already a northern European good.
